question: What was the federal funds target range after each FOMC meeting in 2025, and at which meetings did the Committee change it?
answer:
Taking "each FOMC meeting in 2025" to mean the eight 2025 meetings (January 28-29, March 18-19, May 6-7, June 17-18, July 29-30, September 16-17, October 28-29, and December 9-10, 2025): the federal funds target range started the year at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent and was held there for the first five meetings, then was cut 25 basis points (1/4 percentage point) at each of the last three meetings, ending the year at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. The Committee changed the range at exactly three meetings — September 16-17, October 28-29, and December 9-10, 2025 — each a 25-basis-point cut of both the lower and upper bounds.

| Meeting | Statement date | Target range after meeting | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 28-29, 2025 | Jan 29, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Maintained [D16] |
| Mar 18-19, 2025 | Mar 19, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Maintained [D17] |
| May 6-7, 2025 | May 7, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Maintained [D18] |
| Jun 17-18, 2025 | Jun 18, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Maintained [D19] |
| Jul 29-30, 2025 | Jul 30, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Maintained [D20] |
| Sep 16-17, 2025 | Sep 17, 2025 | 4 to 4-1/4 percent | Cut 25 bps [D21] |
| Oct 28-29, 2025 | Oct 29, 2025 | 3-3/4 to 4 percent | Cut 25 bps [D22] |
| Dec 9-10, 2025 | Dec 10, 2025 | 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent | Cut 25 bps [D23] |

Supporting detail:

- Starting level: The 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent range in force at the start of 2025 was set by the December 18, 2024 meeting, which cut the range 25 bps to that level [D31]. The June 2025 Monetary Policy Report confirms the FOMC "has maintained the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent since the beginning of the year" [D37].
- The five hold meetings (Jan 29, Mar 19, May 7, Jun 18, Jul 30) each state the Committee "decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent" [D16][D17][D18][D19][D20].
- The three cuts each state the Committee "decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point," to 4 to 4-1/4 percent (Sep 17) [D21], to 3-3/4 to 4 percent (Oct 29) [D22], and to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (Dec 10) [D23].
- Effective dates: Each statement was released at 2:00 p.m. on the meeting's second day, with the Implementation Note issued the same day, so the decision was effective on the statement date (Jan 29, Mar 19, May 7, Jun 18, Jul 30, Sep 17, Oct 29, Dec 10, 2025) [D16][D17][D18][D19][D20][D21][D22][D23].
- Post-2025 check: The July 2026 Monetary Policy Report states the FOMC "has maintained the target range for the federal funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent since the beginning of the year," consistent with the December 10, 2025 cut [D40].

Voting context (not required, but noted where the range was contested): at the July 30 hold, Bowman and Waller dissented, preferring a 25-bps cut [D20][D8]; at the September 17 cut, Miran dissented, preferring a 50-bps cut [D21][D11]; at the October 29 cut, Miran preferred 50 bps and Schmid preferred no change [D22][D13]; at the December 10 cut, Miran preferred 50 bps and Goolsbee and Schmid preferred no change [D23][D15].

Note on data cross-check: The FRED series DFEDTARL (lower bound) and DFEDTARU (upper bound) are the standard series for the federal funds target range limits [D26][D27], but the daily FRED values themselves were not available in the sources reviewed, so the figures above are taken directly from the FOMC statements and the Monetary Policy Reports rather than a series-level pull. No discrepancies were found among the statements.

data.answer: The FRED series DFEDTARL/DFEDTARU are not stored as SQL tables in this local collection (I searched table names and titles for dfedt/fedtar/target-range series and found none), so I could not pull the daily FRED values directly. However, the FOMC statements for all eight 2025 meetings are in the collection and state the target range in effect after each meeting, which is exactly what DFEDTARL/DFEDTARU record (effective the day after each meeting, per the FOMC's domestic policy directive). The 2025 path is: 4.25–4.50% from Jan 29 through Jul 30 (five hold meetings), then 4.00–4.25% from Sep 17, 3.75–4.00% from Oct 29, and 3.50–3.75% from Dec 10. Three meetings changed the range, each a 25 bp cut of both bounds: Sep 16–17 (4.25→4.00 lower, 4.50→4.25 upper), Oct 28–29 (4.00→3.75, 4.25→4.00), and Dec 9–10 (3.75→3.50, 4.00→3.75). The Jan 28–29, Mar 18–19, May 6–7, Jun 17–18, and Jul 29–30 meetings all held the range at 4.25–4.50% (the level set by the Dec 18, 2024 cut). These statement values are internally consistent and match the Monetary Policy Reports (June 2025: range held at 4¼–4½% since the beginning of the year; July 2026: range at 3½–3¾% since the beginning of 2026), so they should cross-check cleanly against DFEDTARL/DFEDTARU.
key_facts: Jan 28–29, 2025: maintained target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent (DFEDTARL 4.25, DFEDTARU 4.50, effective Jan 29) [D1]
Mar 18–19, 2025: maintained at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent (effective Mar 19); Waller voted against, supporting no change [D2]

question: Who dissented at each FOMC meeting in 2025, and what did each dissenter prefer?
answer:
Taking "each FOMC meeting in 2025" to mean the eight regular meetings (January 28–29, March 18–19, May 6–7, June 17–18, July 29–30, September 16–17, October 28–29, and December 9–10): five meetings had dissents and three were unanimous. The dissents split into two camps—those who wanted a larger cut (Miran, and Bowman/Waller in July) and those who wanted no cut (Waller in March, and Schmid and Goolsbee in October/December).

| Meeting (2025) | Committee action | Dissenter(s) | What dissenter(s) preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 28–29 | Maintain at 4¼–4½% | None (unanimous) | — [D33][D17] |
| Mar 18–19 | Maintain at 4¼–4½% | Christopher J. Waller | No change to the rate, but continue the current pace of securities-holdings reduction (rather than slow it) [D3][D19] |
| May 6–7 | Maintain at 4¼–4½% | None (unanimous) | — [D21][D5] |
| Jun 17–18 | Maintain at 4¼–4½% | None (unanimous) | — [D23] |
| Jul 29–30 | Maintain at 4¼–4½% | Michelle W. Bowman; Christopher J. Waller | Both preferred to lower the target range by ¼ point at the meeting (to 4–4¼%) [D8][D25] |
| Sep 16–17 | Cut ¼ point to 4–4¼% | Stephen I. Miran | Lower the target range by ½ point at the meeting [D11][D27] |
| Oct 28–29 | Cut ¼ point to 3¾–4% | Stephen I. Miran; Jeffrey R. Schmid | Miran: lower by ½ point; Schmid: no change [D13][D29] |
| Dec 9–10 | Cut ¼ point to 3½–3¾% | Stephen I. Miran; Austan D. Goolsbee; Jeffrey R. Schmid | Miran: lower by ½ point; Goolsbee and Schmid: no change [D15][D31]

Details by meeting:

- **January 28–29:** Unanimous; the Committee maintained the target range at 4¼ to 4½ percent, with "Voting against this action: None" [D33][D17].
- **March 18–19:** One dissent. Christopher J. Waller voted against the decision to maintain the target range at 4¼ to 4½ percent; he supported no change to the rate but preferred to continue the current pace of decline in securities holdings, citing reserve balances over $3 trillion and no sign the banking system was near an ample level of reserves [D3][D19].
- **May 6–7:** Unanimous; maintained at 4¼ to 4½ percent, "Voting against this action: None" (Neel Kashkari voted as an alternate member) [D21][D5].
- **June 17–18:** Unanimous; maintained at 4¼ to 4½ percent, "Voting against this action: None" [D23].
- **July 29–30:** Two dissents. Michelle W. Bowman and Christopher J. Waller both preferred to lower the target range by ¼ point at the meeting (to 4 to 4¼ percent); Adriana D. Kugler was absent and not voting [D8][D25].
- **September 16–17:** One dissent. Stephen I. Miran preferred to lower the target range by ½ point at the meeting, while the Committee cut ¼ point to 4 to 4¼ percent [D11][D27].
- **October 28–29:** Two dissents. Stephen I. Miran preferred to lower the target range by ½ point, and Jeffrey R. Schmid preferred no change; the Committee cut ¼ point to 3¾ to 4 percent [D13][D29].
- **December 9–10:** Three dissents. Stephen I. Miran preferred to lower the target range by ½ point, while Austan D. Goolsbee and Jeffrey R. Schmid preferred no change; the Committee cut ¼ point to 3½ to 3¾ percent [D15][D31].

Note: The evidence covers all eight regular 2025 meetings; no additional (emergency) meetings in 2025 are addressed.

question: How did the Beige Book's overall assessment of economic activity change across the eight editions of 2024?
answer:
Taking "the eight editions of 2024" to refer to the eight editions for which evidence is provided (January, March, April, May, July, September, October, and December), the Beige Book's overall assessment of economic activity followed a pattern of initial stagnation, a period of slight expansion in the spring, a notable softening in the summer and early fall, and a modest rebound by year-end. The tone shifted from "little or no change" in January to "continued to expand" by May, then deteriorated to "little changed" by October before improving to "rose slightly" in December.

*Note: The Federal Reserve typically publishes the Beige Book eight times per year. The evidence provided covers eight specific editions but does not include a June 2024 edition. If a June edition was published in 2024, it is not covered by the available evidence and is therefore excluded from the table below.*

Here is the progression across the eight editions covered by the evidence, in chronological order:

| Edition Date | Overall Assessment | Key Drivers & Context |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jan 17, 2024** | **Little or no change** in a majority of Districts; three reported modest growth, one a moderate decline [D25]. | Strong holiday consumer spending; increased leisure travel; decreases in manufacturing in nearly all Districts; high interest rates limiting auto sales and real estate; optimism about falling rates [D25]. |
| **Mar 6, 2024** | **Increased slightly**, on balance; eight Districts reported slight-to-modest growth, three no change, one slight softening [D35]. | Consumer spending on retail goods inched down; heightened price sensitivity and trade-down behavior; robust air travel but softening restaurant/hotel demand; manufacturing largely unchanged; pickup in residential real estate demand on lower mortgage rates; weak commercial real estate (office) [D35]. |
| **Apr 17, 2024** | **Expanded slightly**, on balance; ten of twelve Districts reported slight or modest growth (up from eight in March), two no change [D36]. | Consumer spending barely increased with weakness in discretionary spending; auto spending buoyed in some Districts by improved inventories and dealer incentives; tourism up modestly; manufacturing declined slightly; bank lending roughly flat; residential construction up a little; cautiously optimistic outlook [D36]. |
| **May 29, 2024** | **Continued to expand** from early April to mid-May; most Districts reported slight or modest growth, two no change [D37]. | Retail spending flat to up slightly on lower discretionary spending and price sensitivity; auto sales roughly flat; travel/tourism strengthened; nonfinancial services demand rose; manufacturing flat to up; tight credit standards and high interest rates constraining lending; housing demand up modestly; commercial real estate softened; outlooks grew "somewhat more pessimistic amid reports of rising uncertainty and greater downside risks" [D37]. |
| **Jul 17, 2024** | **Maintained a slight to modest pace of growth** in a majority of Districts; seven Districts reported increases, five noted flat or declining activity (three more than the prior period) [D27]. | Modest-to-moderate wage growth; modest price rises; little-changed household spending; soft consumer/business loan demand; auto sales weighed down by a dealership cyberattack and high interest rates; expectations of slower growth over six months due to election, domestic policy, geopolitical, and inflation uncertainty [D27]. |
| **Sep 4, 2024** | **Grew slightly in three Districts**; the number of Districts reporting flat or declining activity rose from five to nine [D29]. | Steady employment with rare layoffs; modest wage growth; consumer spending ticked down; manufacturing declined in most Districts; mixed real estate; contacts generally expected activity to remain stable or improve somewhat [D29]. |
| **Oct 23, 2024** | **Little changed** in nearly all Districts since early September; two Districts reported modest growth [D31]. | Declining manufacturing; mixed consumer spending (shift toward cheaper alternatives); housing holding up but mortgage-rate uncertainty and unaffordability; flat commercial real estate (boosted by data center/infrastructure projects); minor dockworkers-strike disruptions; Hurricane damage in the Southeast; somewhat more optimistic longer-term outlook [D31]. |
| **Dec 4, 2024** | **Rose slightly** in most Districts; three regions exhibited modest or moderate growth that offset flat or slightly declining activity in two others [D33]. | Rising growth expectations; stable consumer spending with greater price/quality sensitivity; low mortgage demand amid rate volatility; subdued commercial real estate lending; flat/declining capital spending; weak farm-equipment sales; robust electricity demand driven by data-center expansion [D33]. |

**Summary of the 2024 Trajectory:**
*   **Q1 (Jan–Mar):** Activity was flat to slightly positive, with consumer spending showing early signs of price sensitivity and trade-down behavior [D25][D35].
*   **Q2 (Apr–May):** Expansion was most evident, with the number of Districts reporting growth rising to ten of twelve in April [D36]. However, by May, while activity still "continued to expand," outlooks began to turn "somewhat more pessimistic" due to rising uncertainty [D37].
*   **Q3 (Jul–Sep):** A clear softening occurred. The number of Districts reporting flat or declining activity increased sharply, reaching nine of twelve by September, driven by declining manufacturing and ticking down consumer spending [D27][D29].
*   **Q4 (Oct–Dec):** Activity remained "little changed" in October [D31] but showed a modest rebound in December, with most Districts reporting slight growth and rising expectations for future demand [D33].

Throughout the year, recurring themes included heightened consumer price sensitivity, the constraining effect of high interest rates on housing and auto sales, and weakness in manufacturing and commercial real estate (particularly office space). The provided evidence for the "Overall Economic Activity" sections of these eight editions does not mention tariffs as a driver.

data.answer: The "Overall Economic Activity" section of the National Summary in each of the last four 2024 Beige Book editions shows a gradual softening through the year, then a modest rebound by December. (1) July 17, 2024: activity "maintained a slight to modest pace of growth in a majority of Districts," with seven Districts reporting increases and five flat/declining (three more than the prior period); drivers included modest-to-moderate wage growth, modest price rises, little-changed household spending, soft consumer/business loan demand, auto sales weighed down by a dealership cyberattack and high interest rates, and expectations of slower growth over six months due to election, domestic policy, geopolitical, and inflation uncertainty [D27]. (2) September 4, 2024: activity "grew slightly in three Districts," while flat/declining Districts rose from five to nine; drivers included steady employment with rare layoffs, modest wage growth, consumer spending ticking down, declining manufacturing in most Districts, and mixed real estate, with contacts generally expecting activity to remain stable or improve somewhat [D29]. (3) October 23, 2024: activity was "little changed in nearly all Districts since early September," with two reporting modest growth; drivers included declining manufacturing, mixed consumer spending (shift toward cheaper alternatives), housing holding up but mortgage-rate uncertainty and unaffordability, flat commercial real estate (boosted by data center/infrastructure projects), minor dockworkers-strike disruptions, Hurricane damage in the Southeast, and somewhat more optimistic longer-term outlooks [D31]. (4) December 4, 2024: activity "rose slightly in most Districts," with three regions showing modest/moderate growth offsetting flat/slightly declining activity in two; drivers included rising growth expectations, stable consumer spending with greater price/quality sensitivity, low mortgage demand amid rate volatility, subdued commercial real estate lending, flat/declining capital spending, weak farm-equipment sales, and robust electricity demand driven by data-center expansion [D33].

question: How did the Financial Stability Reports from May 2023 to May 2026 characterize asset valuations?
answer:
Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) from May 2023 to May 2026, the Federal Reserve characterized asset valuations as moving from "moderate" pressures to "elevated" or "stretched" levels relative to fundamentals, with a brief period of "notable" valuations despite price declines in April 2025. Equities and residential real estate were consistently identified as the most stretched asset classes, while commercial real estate (CRE) remained a persistent weak spot with declining prices, and corporate credit spreads moved from near historical averages to low levels.

### Overall Characterization of Asset Valuations

The reports tracked a clear progression in the severity of valuation pressures:

*   **May 2023:** "Asset valuation pressures remained moderate despite notable fluctuations in financial markets" [D2].
*   **October 2023:** "Asset valuation pressures rose to a notable level" [D4].
*   **April 2024:** "Asset valuations increased to elevated levels relative to fundamentals" [D7].
*   **November 2024:** "Asset valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals" [D10].
*   **April 2025:** "Asset valuations were notable despite price declines in some markets in early April" [D22].
*   **November 2025:** "Asset valuations were elevated, with some markets setting new highs after recovering from April’s declines" [D25].
*   **May 2026:** "Asset valuations remained elevated, although risk premiums increased in several markets amid periods of higher volatility" [D28].

### Asset-Specific Valuations

#### Equities
Equity valuations were the most consistently stretched asset class across all seven reports.
*   **May 2023:** Equity prices relative to expected earnings remained above their historical median [D1].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations increased modestly from an already high level [D4].
*   **April 2024:** The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio sat in the upper end of its historical distribution since 1989, and the equity premium stood well below its historical median [D8].
*   **November 2024:** The P/E ratio continued to climb, and the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D11].
*   **April 2025:** Despite equity prices falling more than 6% from the previous FSR due to trade-policy volatility, prices remained high relative to forecasted earnings, and valuations were described as "stretched by historical standards through March" [D22][D24].
*   **November 2025:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D27].
*   **May 2026:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium moved up slightly from an overall low level [D30].

#### Residential Real Estate
Residential valuations were persistently characterized as "elevated" or "increasingly stretched" relative to rents and fundamentals in every report.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near all-time highs despite weakening activity [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations were "increasingly stretched," with the median price-to-rent ratio near its mid-2000s peak [D6].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations remained near peak levels seen in the mid-2000s and were "increasingly stretched" [D7][D9].
*   **November 2024:** Valuations remained near mid-2000s peak levels and "remained stretched" [D10][D12].
*   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals continued to be well above historical averages [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, though at a lower rate (nominal house prices grew 0.3–1.7% in the year ending July 2025) [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, even as house price growth continued to slow [D28].

#### Corporate Credit
Corporate credit spreads moved from near historical averages to low levels, indicating stretched valuations.
*   **May 2023:** Risk premiums stayed near the middle of their historical distributions [D1].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads were somewhat below historical averages [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Spreads narrowed to the lower range of their historical distributions, appearing "stretched" [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Corporate debt markets remained "stretched" [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads widened significantly but stayed at or below historical medians [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads narrowed and stayed well below historical medians [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Corporate bond and loan spreads continued to be low by historical standards [D28].

#### Commercial Real Estate (CRE)
CRE was the persistent weak spot, with prices falling and repeated warnings about distressed sales.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near historically high levels, but price declines were widespread, and fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Rental income relative to property prices remained low from a historical perspective, with especially weak fundamentals in the office sector [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Market conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office, with prices declining against high vacancy and weakening rents [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office and multifamily sectors [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Markets showed some signs of stabilizing, but the potential for distressed sales remained if borrowers could not refinance [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D28].

### Notable Episodic Risks and Liquidity
The reports highlighted specific episodic risks that affected valuations and liquidity:
*   **March 2023 Bank Strains:** The May 2023 report noted significant strains in the banking sector led to notable fluctuations in financial asset prices and liquidity strains in short-term Treasury markets [D2].
*   **August 2024 Yen-Carry Trade Unwind:** The November 2024 report noted that investors exiting the yen-carry trade contributed to a temporary spike in market volatility at the start of August 2024 [D10].
*   **April 2025 Trade-Policy Shock:** The April 2025 report detailed how trade-policy announcements sparked a wave of price declines and volatility, with equity prices falling more than 6% and option-implied volatility reaching levels not seen since March 2020 [D22][D24]. The November 2025 report noted that these price declines largely reversed and volatility receded [D25].

### CRE Price Growth and Market Size Data
The reports provided specific data on CRE price growth (real) and nominal market size in their Table 1.1:

data.answer: Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (May 2023 → May 2026), the Asset Valuations section tracked a clear arc: from "moderate" pressures in May 2023, rising to "notable" (Oct 2023) and "elevated relative to fundamentals" (Apr 2024, Nov 2024), then "notable despite price declines" amid the April 2025 trade-policy shock, "elevated" with new highs after recovery (Nov 2025), and "remained elevated" with higher risk premiums in several markets (May 2026). Residential real estate valuations were persistently "elevated"/"increasingly stretched" relative to rents and fundamentals in every report. data.answer:
Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) from May 2023 to May 2026, the Federal Reserve characterized asset valuations as moving from "moderate" pressures to "elevated" or "stretched" levels relative to fundamentals, with a brief period of "notable" valuations despite price declines in April 2025. Equities and residential real estate were consistently identified as the most stretched asset classes, while commercial real estate (CRE) remained a persistent weak spot with declining prices, and corporate credit spreads moved from near historical averages to low levels.

### Overall Characterization of Asset Valuations

The reports tracked a clear progression in the severity of valuation pressures:

*   **May 2023:** "Asset valuation pressures remained moderate despite notable fluctuations in financial markets" [D2].
*   **October 2023:** "Asset valuation pressures rose to a notable level" [D4].
*   **April 2024:** "Asset valuations increased to elevated levels relative to fundamentals" [D7].
*   **November 2024:** "Asset valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals" [D10].
*   **April 2025:** "Asset valuations were notable despite price declines in some markets in early April" [D22].
*   **November 2025:** "Asset valuations were elevated, with some markets setting new highs after recovering from April’s declines" [D25].
*   **May 2026:** "Asset valuations remained elevated, although risk premiums increased in several markets amid periods of higher volatility" [D28].

### Asset-Specific Valuations

#### Equities
Equity valuations were the most consistently stretched asset class across all seven reports.
*   **May 2023:** Equity prices relative to expected earnings remained above their historical median [D1].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations increased modestly from an already high level [D4].
*   **April 2024:** The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio sat in the upper end of its historical distribution since 1989, and the equity premium stood well below its historical median [D8].
*   **November 2024:** The P/E ratio continued to climb, and the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D11].
*   **April 2025:** Despite equity prices falling more than 6% from the previous FSR due to trade-policy volatility, prices remained high relative to forecasted earnings, and valuations were described as "stretched by historical standards through March" [D22][D24].
*   **November 2025:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D27].
*   **May 2026:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium moved up slightly from an overall low level [D30].

#### Residential Real Estate
Residential valuations were persistently characterized as "elevated" or "increasingly stretched" relative to rents and fundamentals in every report.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near all-time highs despite weakening activity [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations were "increasingly stretched," with the median price-to-rent ratio near its mid-2000s peak [D6].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations remained near peak levels seen in the mid-2000s and were "increasingly stretched" [D7][D9].
*   **November 2024:** Valuations remained near mid-2000s peak levels and "remained stretched" [D10][D12].
*   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals continued to be well above historical averages [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, though at a lower rate (nominal house prices grew 0.3–1.7% in the year ending July 2025) [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, even as house price growth continued to slow [D28].

#### Corporate Credit
Corporate credit spreads moved from near historical averages to low levels, indicating stretched valuations.
*   **May 2023:** Risk premiums stayed near the middle of their historical distributions [D1].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads were somewhat below historical averages [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Spreads narrowed to the lower range of their historical distributions, appearing "stretched" [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Corporate debt markets remained "stretched" [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads widened significantly but stayed at or below historical medians [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads narrowed and stayed well below historical medians [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Corporate bond and loan spreads continued to be low by historical standards [D28].

#### Commercial Real Estate (CRE)
CRE was the persistent weak spot, with prices falling and repeated warnings about distressed sales.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near historically high levels, but price declines were widespread, and fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Rental income relative to property prices remained low from a historical perspective, with especially weak fundamentals in the office sector [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Market conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office, with prices declining against high vacancy and weakening rents [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office and multifamily sectors [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Markets showed some signs of stabilizing, but the potential for distressed sales remained if borrowers could not refinance [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D28].

### Notable Episodic Risks and Liquidity
The reports highlighted specific episodic risks that affected valuations and liquidity:
*   **March 2023 Bank Strains:** The May 2023 report noted significant strains in the banking sector led to notable fluctuations in financial asset prices and liquidity strains in short-term Treasury markets [D2].
*   **August 2024 Yen-Carry Trade Unwind:** The November 2024 report noted that investors exiting the yen-carry trade contributed to a temporary spike in market volatility at the start of August 2024 [D10].
*   **April 2025 Trade-Policy Shock:** The April 2025 report detailed how trade-policy announcements sparked a wave of price declines and volatility, with equity prices falling more than 6% and option-implied volatility reaching levels not seen since March 2020 [D22][D24]. The November 2025 report noted that these price declines largely reversed and volatility receded [D25].

### CRE Price Growth Data
The reports provided specific data on CRE price growth (real) in their Table 1.1:
*   **2023:** −2.9% (reported in the April 2024 FSR) [D23].
*   **2024:** −2.2% (reported in the November 2025 FSR) [D26].
*   **2025:** −1.5% (reported in the May 2026 FSR) [D29].

The CRE nominal market size shrank from $21,676 billion in 2024 to $20,524 billion in 2025, then recovered to $22,083 billion in 2025:Q4 [D23][D26][D29].

issues: The draft states that the CRE nominal market size 'recovered to $22,083 billion in 2025:Q4' [D29], but the evidence in [D29] shows the outstanding amount for Commercial Real Estate is $22,083 billion as of 2025:Q4, while the growth rate for the period 2024:Q4–2025:Q4 is +1.8%. The draft's phrasing implies a recovery from the 2025:Q2 low of $20,524 billion [D26], which is consistent, but the draft previously listed the 2024 value as $21,676 billion [D23]. The sequence $21,676 (2024:Q4) -> $20,524 (2025:Q2) -> $22,083 (2025:Q4) is supported by the tables, but the draft's summary sentence 'shrank from $21,676 billion in 2024 to $20,524 billion in 2025, then recovered to $22,083 billion in 2025:Q4' is slightly imprecise because $21,676 is the 2024:Q4 value, not the full year 2024 average, and the 'recovery' to $22,083 is a year-over-year comparison to 2024:Q4, not necessarily a sequential recovery from 2025:Q2 without intermediate data. However, the most significant error is in the 'CRE Price Growth Data' section.

The draft lists '2023: −2.9% (reported in the April 2024 FSR) [D23]'. The evidence [D23] (April 2025 FSR, not April 2024) shows CRE price growth (real) for the period 2023:Q4–2024:Q4 is -2.9%. The draft attributes this to the April 2024 FSR, which is incorrect; the April 2024 FSR would report data through 2023:Q4. The -2.9% figure is from the April 2025 FSR [D23].

The draft lists '2024: −2.2% (reported in the November 2025 FSR) [D26]'. The evidence [D26] (November 2025 FSR) shows CRE price growth (real) for the period 2024:Q2–2025:Q2 is -2.2%. The draft labels this as '2024', which is ambiguous but likely refers to the year ending in the report's data period. However, the previous point attributed the -2.9% to 2023. The -2.9% in [D23] is for 2023:Q4-2024:Q4. The -2.2% in [D26] is for 2024:Q2-2025:Q2. The draft's labeling of these as '2023' and '2024' is inconsistent with the specific periods in the tables (which are year-over-year or specific quarter ranges). More critically, the draft claims the -2.9% was reported in the April 2024 FSR, but [D23] is the April 2025 FSR.

The draft states 'The CRE nominal market size shrank from $21,676 billion in 2024 to $20,524 billion in 2025'. [D23] shows $21,676 billion as of 2024:Q4. [D26] shows $20,524 billion as of 2025:Q2. This is a valid comparison of those specific points in time. However, the draft then says 'then recovered to $22,083 billion in 2025:Q4 [D29]'. [D29] shows $22,083 billion as of 2025:Q4. This is supported. The main issue is the misattribution of the source report for the -2.9% figure.

*   **April 2025:** Despite equity prices falling more than 6% from the previous FSR due to trade-policy volatility, prices remained high relative to forecasted earnings, and valuations were described as "stretched by historical standards through March" [D22][D24].
*   **November 2025:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D27].
*   **May 2026:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median, and the equity premium moved up slightly from an overall low level [D30].

#### Residential Real Estate
Residential valuations were persistently characterized as "elevated" or "increasingly stretched" relative to rents and fundamentals in every report.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near all-time highs despite weakening activity [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations were "increasingly stretched," with the median price-to-rent ratio near its mid-2000s peak [D6].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations remained near peak levels seen in the mid-2000s and were "increasingly stretched" [D7][D9].
*   **November 2024:** Valuations remained near mid-2000s peak levels and "remained stretched" [D10][D12].
*   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals continued to be well above historical averages [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, though at a lower rate (nominal house prices grew 0.3–1.7% in the year ending July 2025) [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, even as house price growth continued to slow [D28].

#### Corporate Credit
Corporate credit spreads moved from near historical averages to low levels, indicating stretched valuations.
*   **May 2023:** Risk premiums stayed near the middle of their historical distributions [D1].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads were somewhat below historical averages [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Spreads narrowed to the lower range of their historical distributions, appearing "stretched" [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Corporate debt markets remained "stretched" [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads widened significantly but stayed at or below historical medians [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads narrowed and stayed well below historical medians [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Corporate bond and loan spreads continued to be low by historical standards [D28].

#### Commercial Real Estate (CRE)
CRE was the persistent weak spot, with prices falling and repeated warnings about distressed sales.
*   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near historically high levels, but price declines were widespread, and fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D2].
*   **October 2023:** Rental income relative to property prices remained low from a historical perspective, with especially weak fundamentals in the office sector [D4].
*   **April 2024:** Market conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office, with prices declining against high vacancy and weakening rents [D7].
*   **November 2024:** Conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office and multifamily sectors [D10].
*   **April 2025:** Markets showed some signs of stabilizing, but the potential for distressed sales remained if borrowers could not refinance [D22].
*   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D25].
*   **May 2026:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same refinance risk warning [D28].

### Notable Episodic Risks and Liquidity
The reports highlighted specific episodic risks that affected valuations and liquidity:
*   **March 2023 Bank Strains:** The May 2023 report noted significant strains in the banking sector led to notable fluctuations in financial asset prices and liquidity strains in short-term Treasury markets [D2].
*   **August 2024 Yen-Carry Trade Unwind:** The November 2024 report noted that investors exiting the yen-carry trade contributed to a temporary spike in market volatility at the start of August 2024 [D10].
*   **April 2025 Trade-Policy Shock:** The April 2025 report detailed how trade-policy announcements sparked a wave of price declines and volatility, with equity prices falling more than 6% and option-implied volatility reaching levels not seen since March 2020 [D22][D24]. The November 2025 report noted that these price declines largely reversed and volatility receded [D25].

question: How did FOMC participants' median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate change across the Summaries of Economic Projections from March 2025 to September 2026?
answer:
The median FOMC projection for the 2026 civilian unemployment rate was revised down by a total of 0.2 percentage points over the period, moving from 4.3% in the March 2025 SEP to 4.1% in the September 2026 SEP. The path was not monotonic: the projection first rose to 4.5% in June 2025, then eased to 4.4% by September 2025, held steady through March 2026, and declined to 4.3% in June 2026 and 4.1% in September 2026.

| SEP release (meeting date) | Median 2026 unemployment rate | Change from prior SEP |
|---|---|---|
| March 19, 2025 | 4.3% | — |
| June 18, 2025 | 4.5% | +0.2 pp |
| September 17, 2025 | 4.4% | −0.1 pp |
| December 10, 2025 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp |
| March 18, 2026 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp |
| June 17, 2026 | 4.3% | −0.1 pp |
| September 16, 2026 | 4.1% | −0.2 pp |

Source and notes:
- The values above are the "Median" row, 2026 column of SEP Table 1 for each meeting, drawn directly from the SEP documents [D1][D2]. All seven meetings in the requested window (March 2025 through September 2026) are covered.
- These are projections for the average civilian unemployment rate in the fourth quarter of 2026, per the SEP Table 1 definitions [W2].
- The FRED Blog summaries corroborate the series: March 2025 (4.3% for 2026) [W13], December 2025 (4.4% by Q4 2026, "largely unchanged from the September projection") [W12], March 2026 (4.4% in Q4 2026) [W1], June 2026 (4.3% in Q4 2026) [W9], and September 2026 (4.1% in Q4 2026) [W10].
- One discrepancy: the June 2025 SEP Table 1 median for 2026 is 4.5% [D1][D2], whereas the June 2025 FRED Blog does not explicitly state the 2026 figure in its text; it notes the median projects the rate will "average 4.5% in Q4 2025 and drop to 4.4% by 2027," which is consistent with a 2026 value of 4.5% (or 4.4%) but does not specify it [W15]. The official SEP Table 1 value of 4.5% is used here.
- The net change (4.1% − 4.3% = −0.2 pp) equals the sum of the six period-over-period changes (+0.2 − 0.1 + 0.0 + 0.0 − 0.1 − 0.2), confirming internal consistency [D1][D2].

data.answer:
The FOMC's median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate ended the period 0.2 percentage points lower than it began, falling from 4.3% in the March 2025 Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) to 4.1% in the September 2026 SEP. The path was not monotonic: the projection first rose, then held steady for two meetings, and finally declined over the last three meetings.

| SEP meeting (date) | Median 2026 unemployment rate | Change vs. prior SEP |
|---|---|---|
| March 19, 2025 | 4.3% | — |
| June 18, 2025 | 4.5% | +0.2 pp |
| September 17, 2025 | 4.4% | −0.1 pp |
| December 10, 2025 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp |
| March 18, 2026 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp |
| June 17, 2026 | 4.3% | −0.1 pp |
| September 16, 2026 | 4.1% | −0.2 pp |

[1]

Key points:
- The only upward revision in the window was at the June 18, 2025 meeting, when the median 2026 unemployment rate was raised from 4.3% to 4.5% [1].
- The projection then came back down to 4.4% at the September 17, 2025 meeting and stayed at 4.4% through the December 10, 2025 and March 18, 2026 meetings [1].
- It was trimmed to 4.3% at the June 17, 2026 meeting and to 4.1% at the September 16, 2026 meeting, the lowest level in the series [1].
- Net change from March 2025 (4.3%) to September 2026 (4.1%) is −0.2 percentage points [1].

Note: The figures above are the "Median" 2026 values from SEP Table 1 as of each meeting. The same tables also report the prior meeting's projection for 2026 (e.g., the September 2026 SEP lists the June 2026 projection of 4.3% for 2026), which is consistent with the sequence shown [1].

question: Which Federal Reserve Governors gave speeches on stablecoins or tokenization in 2025 and 2026, and what was each one's main point?
answer:
Taking "2025 and 2026" to mean speeches delivered in calendar years 2025 and 2026, the evidence identifies three Federal Reserve Governors who spoke on stablecoins or tokenization in that window: Michael S. Barr, Christopher J. Waller, and Stephen I. Miran. The evidence does not cover any speeches by other Governors (e.g., Bowman, Cook, Jefferson, Kugler) on these topics in 2025–2026.

**Governors and their main points**

| Governor | Speech / Venue | Year | Main point on stablecoins/tokenization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Michael S. Barr | "Exploring the Possibilities and Risks of New Payment Technologies," 2025 D.C. Fintech Week, Washington, D.C. [D10] | 2025 | Stablecoins can improve payment efficiency, especially cross-border, but reaching that potential requires strong guardrails and consumer protections; much will depend on how federal and state regulators implement the GENIUS Act, and he urges considering how tokenized deposits fit into the payments ecosystem [D10]. |
| Stephen I. Miran | "A Global Stablecoin Glut: Implications for Monetary Policy," BCVC Summit 2025, Harvard Club of New York City, New York, New York [D12] | 2025 | Stablecoins are now an established, fast-growing part of the financial landscape (not a "pariah"), and the GENIUS Act—passed "this year" (2025)—provides a clear U.S. regulatory pathway; he argues economic research needs to catch up, particularly on how rapid stablecoin growth affects the supply of loanable funds and monetary policy, and he is encouraged by the Fed's steps to recognize stablecoins' importance for the payment system [D12]. |
| Christopher J. Waller | "Reflections on a Maturing Stablecoin Market," A Very Stable Conference, San Francisco, California [D11] | 2025 or 2026 (not specified) | Stablecoins are a form of private money subject to run risk and payment-system risks, and the market needs a clear, proportionate U.S. regulatory and supervisory framework that addresses those risks directly and allows both banks and non-banks to issue regulated stablecoins, without stifling innovation while the market is still developing [D11]. |
| Michael S. Barr | "Brief Remarks on Stablecoins," "The GENIUS Act in Practice: Key Questions for Stablecoin Regulation," The Federalist Society, Washington, D.C. [D13] | 2026 (inferred) | The GENIUS Act gives issuers needed regulatory clarity and could spur faster stablecoin development, but a key concern is the risk of money laundering/terrorist financing via secondary markets lacking customer-identification requirements, requiring both regulatory and technological solutions; he also notes stablecoins are currently used mostly for crypto-trading and as a dollar store of value abroad, with possible future uses in remittances, trade finance, and treasury management [D13]. |

**Notes on dates and coverage**
- The Barr Fintech Week speech is explicitly dated to 2025 by the venue name "2025 D.C. Fintech Week" [D10].
- The Miran speech is explicitly dated to 2025 by the venue name "BCVC Summit 2025" [D12].
- The Barr "Brief Remarks" speech is inferred to be from 2026: Barr states that Congress passed the GENIUS Act "last year" [D13], while Miran, speaking at the BCVC Summit 2025, states the Act was passed "this year" [D12]. Since the Act was passed in 2025, Barr's reference to it as "last year" places his speech in 2026. The evidence does not provide an explicit calendar date for this speech [D13].
- The evidence does not provide a specific year for the Waller speech; it is listed without a date in the available excerpts [D11].
- No evidence was found for speeches on stablecoins or tokenization in 2025–2026 by Governors Bowman, Cook, Jefferson, or Kugler; the research on those speakers was inconclusive, so I cannot confirm or rule out such speeches for them.

question: How did the Monetary Policy Reports from February 2025 to July 2026 describe the role of tariffs in inflation?
answer:
Taking the question to cover the three Monetary Policy Reports (MPRs) published in that window—the February 7, 2025, June 20, 2025, and July 10, 2026 reports—the description of tariffs' role in inflation evolved sharply: from a near-absence of tariff discussion in February 2025, to tariffs becoming a central, though highly uncertain, driver of goods inflation and short-term expectations in June 2025, to a retrospective assessment in July 2026 that tariff hikes had "contributed in part" to the 2025 upturn in consumer goods prices, with the tariff pass-through largely unwinding in 2026 after a Supreme Court ruling. None of the three reports provides a single quantitative estimate (e.g., percentage points) of tariffs' contribution to headline or core inflation; all rely on qualitative and category-level evidence.

| Report (date) | How tariffs are described in relation to inflation | Key language / evidence | Quantitative estimate? |
|---|---|---|---|
| February 7, 2025 MPR | Tariffs are essentially absent from the inflation discussion. They appear only twice, in International Developments, as a forward-looking "prospect" affecting capital flows and the dollar—not as a current driver of U.S. prices. The inflation section attributes a small boost to core goods to rising nonfuel import prices without naming tariffs. | EME fund outflows in Q4 2024 as investors reacted to "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." [D38]; "Some market participants also pointed to potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar higher" [D39]; core goods "received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year," with no explicit tariff attribution [D15]. The Summary and Monetary Policy sections contain no tariff mention [D35][D40]. | No. |
| June 20, 2025 MPR | Tariffs become a central factor in the inflation outlook, but their pass-through is characterized as highly uncertain. The report finds evidence tariffs "may have contributed" to the upturn in goods inflation, raised input costs, and lifted short-term inflation expectations, while noting foreign producers had not offset tariffs by cutting prices. | "The effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond" [D22]; "the pattern of net price changes among goods categories this year suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with "somewhat strong" price changes in household appliances and consumer electronics but not new motor vehicles [D22]; "prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum have risen substantially relative to the global prices... likely reflecting the effects of tariffs" [D22]; nonfuel import prices (excluding tariffs) "have increased modestly... suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers" [D22]; firms "widely report... increases in input cost pressures this year, which many firms have linked to higher tariffs" [D22]; "measures of shorter-term inflation expectations have moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs" [D19]; household/business sentiment "declined this year amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" [D19]; Q1 GDP dragged down by "a historic surge in imports ahead of expected increases in tariffs" [D20]. | No single estimate; the report cites external studies (Minton & Somale 2025; Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez 2025) for quantitative tariff price-impact estimates but does not reproduce a figure [D22]. |
| July 10, 2026 MPR | A retrospective, more confident assessment: earlier tariff hikes "pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" and "contributed in part" to the 2025 upturn in consumer goods prices. The report also notes the tariff effect is fading in 2026 after a Supreme Court ruling invalidated many tariff measures, and that tariffs are a headwind to foreign growth. | Summary: factors "contributing to higher measured prices are earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods, a surge in energy prices... and increased demand for some high-tech products" [D25][D26]; "measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods" [D12]; "the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with higher average monthly price increases in high-import-content categories (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends [D14]; most high-tech goods (computers, semiconductors) are exempt, so "changes in tariff rates are not an important factor in their prices" [D14]; food price step-up partly reflects "the effects of higher tariffs" [D13]; prices paid by domestic producers to import (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year," reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate after February's Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative measures [D32][D43]; Michigan 12-month inflation expectations (4.6% in June) were "still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" [D34]; U.S. tariffs cited as headwinds to foreign growth, with sectoral tariffs "continuing to weigh on manufacturing" in Mexico and Canada [D28][D45]. | No. |

Key points across the series:

- **Trajectory of emphasis.** The February 2025 MPR predates the January 2025 tariff announcements taking effect and treats tariffs only as a future "prospect" in the context of emerging-market fund flows and the dollar [D38][D39]; its inflation discussion does not attribute the small core-goods boost to tariffs [D15]. By June 2025, tariffs are a central, current driver of the inflation outlook, goods inflation, input costs, and short-term expectations, though the Committee stresses the pass-through is "highly uncertain" and "still early to assess" [D22][D19]. By July 2026, the language is retrospective and more definitive—tariffs "contributed in part" to the 2025 goods-price upturn—while noting the effect is receding in 2026 [D12][D14][D32][D43].

- **Consistent methodological caveat.** Both the June 2025 and July 2026 reports state that "the effects of tariffs cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics" and depend on the responses of consumers, firms, importers, and foreign exporters; they infer the tariff effect from the pattern of price changes in high-import-content categories [D22][D14].

- **No quantitative contribution in any report.** None of the three MPRs provides a percentage-point or share estimate of tariffs' contribution to CPI or PCE. The June 2025 report references external Fed and academic studies for such estimates but does not reproduce a number [D22]; the July 2026 report's assessment is entirely qualitative ("contributed in part," "pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods") [D14][D25][D26].

- **Inflation-expectations channel.** The June 2025 report notes shorter-term inflation expectations "moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs," with the University of Michigan 12-month expectation rising from 2.8% in December to 5.1% [D19][D24], while longer-term expectations remained anchored [D19][D24]. The July 2026 report notes Michigan 12-month expectations (4.6% in June) were "still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" [D34], and that most longer-term measures remained consistent with the 2 percent objective [D26][D34].

- **2026 unwinding.** The July 2026 report adds a development not present in the earlier reports: prices paid by domestic producers to import (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year," reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate after February's Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative measures [D32][D43].

Note on coverage: the evidence reviewed covers the Summary, Domestic Developments (inflation), and International Developments sections of each report, which contain all tariff-inflation language found via targeted searches; a brief mention in other sections (e.g., financial stability or special topics boxes) cannot be 100% ruled out, but no additional tariff-inflation passages were identified.

data.answer: The February 7, 2025 Monetary Policy Report (83 pages) does not contain a dedicated section on tariffs and their impact on inflation. Tariffs are mentioned only twice, in the International Developments section, and neither mention quantifies or even qualitatively assesses a tariff contribution to U.S. price increases. First, in the discussion of emerging market fund flows (p. 47), the report notes that EME fund inflows "turned to large outflows in the fourth quarter as investors reacted to the deterioration in the economic outlook for China, rising U.S. longer-term interest rates, and the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." [D38]. Second, in the dollar-exchange-value discussion (p. 48), it states that "Some market participants also pointed to potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar higher in recent months" [D39]. The inflation discussion itself (Summary p. 11 and Domestic Developments pp. 15-19) attributes the small boost to core goods inflation to "price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year" [D15], without explicitly attributing that to tariffs. No quantitative estimate of a tariff contribution to inflation appears anywhere in the report.
key_facts: p. 47 (International Developments): EME fund outflows in Q4 2024 as investors reacted to 'the deterioration in the economic outlook for China, rising U.S. longer-term interest rates, and the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S.' [D38]
p. 48 (International Developments): 'Some market participants also pointed to potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar higher in recent months.' [D39]

p. 17 (Domestic Developments, inflation section): 'Core goods inflation received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year (figure 6).' — no explicit tariff attribution [D15]

Summary (p. 11) and Monetary Policy section (p. 49) contain no mention of tariffs; the FOMC's inflation outlook language refers only to 'incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks' [D35, D40]

The report's table of contents (p. 5) shows no tariff-related section or box; special topics cover employment/earnings, labor productivity, financial stability, balance sheet, periodic review, and monetary policy rules [outline]
data.gaps: I verified the Summary (pp. 11-13), the full inflation discussion (pp. 15-19), the International Developments tariff mentions (pp. 47-48), and the Monetary Policy section (p. 49), and ran multiple targeted searches for 'tariffs', 'tariff pass-through', 'trade policy', 'import prices', and 'tariff announcement'. The only tariff mentions found are the two in International Developments. I did not exhaustively read every page of the 83-page report (e.g., Box 3 financial stability, pp. 42-44), so a stray mention there cannot be 100% ruled out, but searches over the full document returned no additional tariff passages. The report predates the January 2025 tariff announcements taking effect, so it contains no quantitative estimate of tariffs' contribution to inflation.

data.answer: The June 20, 2025 Monetary Policy Report discusses tariffs and inflation in three main places: (1) the Summary (pp. 11–12), (2) the Domestic Developments inflation section (pp. 17–19), and (3) the International Developments summary (p. 13). The report's core language is that "the effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond" [D22]. It finds that "the pattern of net price changes among goods categories this year suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with "somewhat strong" price changes in household appliances and consumer electronics, though not in new motor vehicles [D22]. The report notes that "prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum have risen substantially relative to the global prices, on net, over this period, likely reflecting the effects of tariffs," and that nonfuel import prices (excluding tariffs) "have increased modestly," suggesting foreign producers have not offset tariffs by cutting prices [D22]. Firms "widely report on business surveys that they have faced increases in input cost pressures this year, which many firms have linked to higher tariffs" [D22]. On inflation expectations, the report states "measures of shorter-term inflation expectations have moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs," while longer-term expectations remain anchored [D19]. The Summary also notes household and business sentiment "have declined this year amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" [D19], and that Q1 GDP was dragged down by "a historic surge in imports ahead of expected increases in tariffs" [D20]. No specific quantitative estimate of the tariff pass-through to CPI/PCE is provided; the report relies on qualitative and category-level evidence. Compared to the February 2025 MPR (which mentioned only the "prospect of new U.S. tariffs" in the context of EME fund flows [D2]), the June 2025 report represents a major escalation in emphasis, with tariffs now a central factor in the inflation outlook, goods inflation, input costs, and inflation expectations.
key_facts: "The effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond." (p. 17) [D22]

"nonfuel import prices—which measure the prices paid to foreign producers and exclude tariffs—have increased modestly so far this year, suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers" (p. 17) [D22]
"domestic firms widely report on business surveys that they have faced increases in input cost pressures this year, which many firms have linked to higher tariffs" (p. 17) [D22]
"measures of shorter-term inflation expectations have moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs" (p. 11) [D19]

"a historic surge in imports ahead of expected increases in tariffs" dragged down Q1 GDP (p. 12) [D20]

data.gaps: The full comparison with the February 2025 MPR's inflation section (pp. 15–20) was not fully read, so the tone comparison is based on the limited tariff mentions found in the February report's search results. The July 2024 MPR search returned no relevant tariff passages, suggesting tariffs were not a significant topic in that report. The report references external studies (Minton & Somale 2025; Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez 2025) for quantitative tariff price impact estimates, but those are not reproduced in the MPR itself.

data.answer: The July 10, 2026 Monetary Policy Report discusses tariffs and inflation in four places, all qualitatively — the report provides no quantitative estimate (e.g., percentage-point contribution) of tariffs to inflation. (1) In the Summary (pp. 9–10), the report lists "earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" as one of three factors (alongside the energy price surge from the Middle East conflict and AI-driven high-tech demand) "contributing to higher measured prices" [D25][D26]. (2) In Domestic Developments (p. 13), it states that "measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods" [D12]. (3) In the core goods section (p. 15), the report notes that "the effects of tariffs cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics, and these effects depend on the responses of consumers, firms, importers, and foreign exporters. Nonetheless, the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," citing higher average monthly price increases in high-import-content categories such as household appliances and consumer electronics relative to pre-tariff trends; it also notes that most high-tech goods (computers, semiconductors) are exempt from tariffs, so tariff rates are "not an important factor" in those prices [D14]. (4) On p. 16, the report observes that import prices paid by domestic producers (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year," reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate after February's Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative measures [D32][D43]. Related context: food price increases partly reflect "the effects of higher tariffs" (p. 14) [D13], Michigan 12-month inflation expectations peaked after "last year's announcements of tariff increases" (p. 18) [D34], and U.S. tariffs are cited as a headwind to foreign growth (pp. 11, 41) [D28][D45].
key_facts: Summary (pp. 9-10): factors 'contributing to higher measured prices are earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods, a surge in energy prices... and increased demand for some high-tech products that support AI applications' [D25][D26].

p. 13: 'measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods' [D12].

p. 15: 'The effects of tariffs cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics... the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases'; average monthly price increases were higher in high-import-content categories (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends [D14].
p. 15: most high-tech goods (computers, semiconductors) are exempt from tariffs, so 'changes in tariff rates are not an important factor in their prices' [D14].

p. 16: prices paid by domestic producers to import products (which include tariffs) 'are estimated to have decreased this year,' reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate following February's Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative measures [D32][D43].
p. 14: step-up in measured food price inflation partly reflects 'the effects of higher tariffs and increases in agricultural and livestock commodity prices' [D13].
p. 18: Michigan 12-month inflation expectations (4.6% in June) were 'still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases' [D34].
pp. 11, 41: U.S. tariffs cited as headwinds to foreign economic activity, with sectoral tariffs 'continuing to weigh on manufacturing' in Mexico and Canada [D28][D45].

No quantitative estimate (percentage points or share of inflation) of the tariff contribution appears in the sections reviewed; the report's assessment is qualitative ('contributed in part,' 'pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods').
data.gaps: I reviewed the Summary (pp. 9-12), Domestic Developments inflation sections (pp. 13-18), and International Developments (pp. 41-43), which contain all tariff-inflation language found via multiple targeted searches. I did not exhaustively read the remaining sections (Financial Developments pp. 35-40, Monetary Policy pp. 45-52, Special Topics pp. 12/53-70, and the SEP discussion), so a brief tariff mention in those sections cannot be fully ruled out, though searches for tariff-related phrasing returned no additional passages. The report contains no quantitative tariff contribution estimate in the sections examined.

data.answer:
Taking the question to cover the three Monetary Policy Reports (MPRs) published in that window—the February 7, 2025, June 20, 2025, and July 10, 2026 reports—the description of tariffs' role in inflation evolved sharply: from a near-absence of tariff discussion in February 2025, to tariffs becoming a central, though highly uncertain, driver of goods inflation and short-term expectations in June 2025, to a retrospective assessment in July 2026 that tariff hikes had "contributed in part" to the 2025 upturn in consumer goods prices, with the tariff pass-through largely unwinding in 2026 after a Supreme Court ruling. None of the three reports provides a single quantitative estimate (e.g., percentage points) of tariffs' contribution to headline or core inflation; all rely on qualitative and category-level evidence.

| Report (date) | How tariffs are described in relation to inflation | Key language / evidence | Quantitative estimate? |
|---|---|---|---|
| February 7, 2025 MPR | Tariffs are essentially absent from the inflation discussion. They appear only twice, in International Developments, as a forward-looking "prospect" affecting capital flows and the dollar—not as a current driver of U.S. prices. The inflation section attributes a small boost to core goods to rising nonfuel import prices without naming tariffs. | EME fund outflows in Q4 2024 as investors reacted to "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." [D38]; "Some market participants also pointed to potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar higher" [D39]; core goods "received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year," with no explicit tariff attribution [D15]. The Summary and Monetary Policy sections contain no tariff mention [D35][D40]. | No. |
| June 20, 2025 MPR | Tariffs become a central factor in the inflation outlook, but their pass-through is characterized as highly uncertain. The report finds evidence tariffs "may have contributed" to the upturn in goods inflation, raised input costs, and lifted short-term inflation expectations, while noting foreign producers had not offset tariffs by cutting prices. | "The effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond" [D22]; "the pattern of net price changes among goods categories this year suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with "somewhat strong" price changes in household appliances and consumer electronics but not new motor vehicles [D22]; "prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum have risen substantially relative to the global prices... likely reflecting the effects of tariffs" [D22]; nonfuel import prices (excluding tariffs) "have increased modestly... suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers" [D22]; firms "widely report... increases in input cost pressures this year, which many firms have linked to higher tariffs" [D22]; "measures of shorter-term inflation expectations have moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs" [D19]; household/business sentiment "declined this year amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" [D19]; Q1 GDP dragged down by "a historic surge in imports ahead of expected increases in tariffs" [D20]. | No single estimate; the report cites external studies (Minton & Somale 2025; Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez 2025) for quantitative tariff price-impact estimates but does not reproduce a figure [D22]. |
| July 10, 2026 MPR | A retrospective, more confident assessment: earlier tariff hikes "pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" and "contributed in part" to the 2025 upturn in consumer goods prices. The report also notes the tariff effect is fading in 2026 after a Supreme Court ruling invalidated many tariff measures, and that tariffs are a headwind to foreign growth. | Summary: factors "contributing to higher measured prices are earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods, a surge in energy prices... and increased demand for some high-tech products" [D25][D26]; "measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods" [D12]; "the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with higher average monthly price increases in high-import-content categories (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends [D14]; most high-tech goods (computers, semiconductors) are exempt, so "changes in tariff rates are not an important factor in their prices" [D14]; food price step-up partly reflects "the effects of higher tariffs" [D13]; prices paid by domestic producers to import (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year," reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate after February's Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative measures [D32][D43]; Michigan 12-month inflation expectations (4.6% in June) were "still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" [D34]; U.S. tariffs cited as headwinds to foreign growth, with sectoral tariffs "continuing to weigh on manufacturing" in Mexico and Canada [D28][D45]. | No. |

Key points across the series:

- **Trajectory of emphasis.** The February 2025 MPR predates the January 2025 tariff announcements taking effect and treats tariffs only as a future "prospect" in the context of emerging-market fund flows and the dollar [D38][D39]; its inflation discussion does not attribute the small core-goods boost to tariffs [D15]. By June 2025, tariffs are a central, current driver of the inflation outlook, goods inflation, input costs, and short-term expectations, though the Committee stresses the pass-through is "highly uncertain" and "still early to assess" [D22][D19]. By July 2026, the language is retrospective and more definitive—tariffs "contributed in part" to the 2025 goods-price upturn—while noting the effect is receding in 2026 [D12][D14][D32][D43].

- **Consistent methodological caveat.** Both the June 2025 and July 2026 reports state that "the effects of tariffs cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics" and depend on the responses of consumers, firms, importers, and foreign exporters; they infer the tariff effect from the pattern of price changes in high-import-content categories [D22][D14].

- **No quantitative contribution in any report.** None of the three MPRs provides a percentage-point or share estimate of tariffs' contribution to CPI or PCE. question: What changes to the Federal Reserve Board's membership and leadership happened between January 2025 and September 2026?
answer:
Between January 2025 and September 2026, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors experienced seven distinct membership and leadership changes: the departure of Michael Barr from the Vice Chair for Supervision role, the appointment of Michelle Bowman as Vice Chair for Supervision, the resignation of Adriana Kugler, the appointment and subsequent resignation of Stephen Miran, and the transition of the Chair role from Jerome Powell to Kevin Warsh, which included a brief period where Powell served as chair pro tempore.

The specific events, in chronological order, are as follows:

*   **January 2025:** The Board announced on a Monday that Michael S. Barr would step down as Vice Chair for Supervision, effective February 28, 2025, or earlier upon a successor's confirmation. Barr continued to serve as a governor [D7].
*   **June 9, 2025:** Michelle W. Bowman was sworn in as Vice Chair for Supervision. She had been nominated on March 24, 2025, and confirmed by the Senate on June 4, 2025. Her term as Vice Chair for Supervision ends on June 9, 2029, and her term as a Board member ends on January 31, 2034 [D3].
*   **August 2025:** The Board announced on a Friday that Adriana D. Kugler would resign as a governor, effective August 8, 2025. She had served on the Board since September 13, 2023 [D4].
*   **September 16, 2025:** Stephen I. Miran was sworn in as a member of the Board to fill an unexpired term ending January 31, 2026. He was nominated on September 2, 2025, and confirmed by the Senate on September 15, 2025 [D1].
*   **May 14, 2026:** Stephen I. Miran submitted his resignation as a Board member, effective when or shortly before his successor is sworn in. He had served on the Board since September 16, 2025 [D17].
*   **May 15, 2026:** As Jerome H. Powell's term as chair concluded and the swearing-in of his successor was pending, the Board named Powell as chair pro tempore. This temporary measure is consistent with past practice during chair transitions [D18].
*   **May 22, 2026:** Kevin Warsh took the oath of office as chairman and a member of the Board of Governors. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) also unanimously selected him as its chairman. Warsh was nominated on March 4, 2026, confirmed as a Board member on May 12, 2026, and confirmed as chairman on May 13, 2026. His term as chairman ends on May 21, 2030, and his term as a Board member ends on January 31, 2040 [D19].

These events mark the primary shifts in the Board's composition and leadership hierarchy during the specified period, culminating in Kevin Warsh assuming the role of Chair from Jerome Powell in May 2026.

The specific events, in chronological order, are as follows:

*   **May 22, 2026:** Kevin Warsh took the oath of office as chairman and a member of the Board of Governors. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) also unanimously selected him as its chairman. His term as chairman ends on May 21, 2030, and his term as a Board member ends on January 31, 2040 [D19].

These events mark the primary shifts in the Board's composition and leadership hierarchy during the specified period, culminating in Kevin Warsh assuming the role of Chair from Jerome Powell in May 2026.
